headline: The official same-point comparison now rests on two states and leans Republican relative to the polls: Florida's returned mail ballots were D+6.2 by registration on Oct 16 (816,890 ballots) against D+3.7 at 18 days out in 2022, and Iowa's 1,418 absentee ballots are D+45 against D+10; pooled, the change since 2022 implies a national vote of about D+0.7 with a ±2.1 band, against polls at D+7.7, though Florida's figure is mail only until in-person voting opens Oct 19 and Iowa's count is tiny. North Carolina's official files remain the most Democratic reading: 437,214 ballots accepted through Oct 16 against 326,248 at this point in 2022, with registered Democrats up from 131,674 to 198,547, Republicans down from 98,173 to 90,076, unaffiliated voters up from 95,807 to 147,722 and Black voters up from 58,259 to 100,923. Nevada's mail vote was D+2.7 (46,491 ballots) as in-person voting opens Oct 17, and Jon Ralston's first model projects an R+3 final electorate; Georgia passed 500,000 voters on its third day, but at the same days out its total early vote still trails 2022's.

measures.label: Iowa: early voters by registration, D-minus-R margin (mail plus in person)
measures.src: Call the Map (Iowa Secretary of State daily absentee statistics), Oct 16
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official files; affiliation not stated. 17,385 ballots through Oct 14 vs. the same point in 2024

measures.label: Pennsylvania: returned mail ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin (52 comparable counties)
measures.src: Call the Map (Pennsylvania Department of State mail-ballot file), Oct 16
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 52 of 67 counties (92% of ballots); the app's own comparison takes over once the 2024 baseline reaches this point

measures.label: Maine: absentee ballots by registration, D-minus-R margin
measures.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 16
measures.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated. 47,497 ballots through Oct 12 vs. the same point in 2024

measures.label: Virginia: Democratic share of early voters, two-party (L2 modeled party)
measures.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Virginia has no party registration, so party is modeled in both years

measures.label: Ohio: early voters by party (last primary ballot), D-minus-R margin
measures.src: News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13 (Ohio Secretary of State data)

compare_note: Registered-party margin among early ballots, 2026 vs. the same point in 2024, as read from the official files by Call the Map (an independent tracker; Iowa 17,385 ballots through Oct 14, Pennsylvania's 52 comparable counties, Maine through Oct 12). Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Florida's, Nevada's, Colorado's, Iowa's, Pennsylvania's and North Carolina's official comparisons with 2022 and 2024 are computed from the state files above. Every state with party registration is more Democratic than at this point in 2024, a presidential year in which Republicans moved into early voting; against 2022 the picture is split.

bullets.title: Georgia passed 500,000 voters on day three, but at the same days out its total early vote still trails 2022.
bullets.html: More than half a million Georgians had voted by 5 p.m. on Oct 15, about 6.9% of the state's 7.5 million-plus active voters, with about 21,700 mail ballots accepted and the rest cast in person; day one (188,667) was about 40% above 2022's first day, and 54% of voters so far are women. Yet at the same days out GeorgiaVotes counted 380,948 ballots through Oct 14 against 443,696 in 2022, 14% fewer: 2022's in-person voting opened a day earlier relative to Election Day and its mail vote was several times larger. Georgia has no party registration.
sources: CBS News Atlanta (Secretary of State data), Oct 15
bullets.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state's files

bullets.title: North Carolina's first two days are 34% ahead of 2022, with Democrats up by half and Republicans down.
bullets.html: By the State Board's files, 437,214 ballots had been accepted through Oct 16 (398,581 in person, 38,633 by mail) against 326,248 at the same point in 2022: registered Democrats 198,547 vs. 131,674, Republicans 90,076 vs. 98,173, unaffiliated 147,722 vs. 95,807, and Black voters 100,923 vs. 58,259. Mail is down from 56,355, so the gain is all in person. Bitzer's reading of day one: 48% Democratic, 32% unaffiliated and 20% Republican, two-thirds of them voters in all four general elections since 2018, and 15% under 45 (12% in 2022). The app's own comparison from the State Board's files tracks the same point daily.
sources: NC State Board of Elections via the app's comparison, Oct 16
Call the Map (State Board file through Oct 15), Oct 16
bullets.aff: Official data; nonpartisan academic; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic.
bullets.html: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000, by last primary ballot (Ohio Capital Journal, from Secretary of State data); News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes in the first week were 194,841, nearly four times 2022's 50,368, and Cuyahoga, Lucas, Lorain and Summit counties have already passed 40% of their 2022 early-vote totals; but only 631,079 mail ballots have been requested vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022, and seniors are more than half of the ballots cast.
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

bullets.title: The edge over 2024 is real but partly a change in how Democrats vote.
bullets.html: Democratic mail requests in North Carolina are down 40% from 2022, against 18% for Republicans, yet Democrats are returning ballots faster (22% returned vs. 17% in 2022). In Pennsylvania, 30% of the Democrats who had voted early by this point in 2024 have already voted again, vs. 18% of Republicans (L2 data via G. Elliott Morris). In an NBC poll, 23% of Democrats plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024, and 36% plan to vote early in person, up from 30%.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor

bullets.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is down 30% on 2022; Michigan's has flattened.
bullets.html: Wisconsin clerks had received about 128,000 absentee ballots three weeks out, against nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022; Madison fell from about 31,700 to about 9,000, which Dane County's clerk attributes to distrust of the Postal Service. Michigan's returned absentee ballots (440,677 on Oct 13) are only slightly above the same point in 2022 (432,960), though requests are up more than 20% because of the permanent mail list. Neither state registers voters by party.

bullets.title: Florida's first 2022 match leans Democratic, but the pooled implied margin is far below the polls.
bullets.html: By registration, 816,890 returned mail ballots were D+6.2 on Oct 16 (347,264 Democrats, 296,689 Republicans, 172,937 others) against D+3.7 at 18 days out in 2022, a 2.5-point more Democratic gap that the app's calibrated slope turns into about 2.1 points of margin (±2.4). Pooled with Iowa (D+45 vs. D+10 in 2022 on 1,418 ballots), the official comparison implies a national vote of about D+0.7 ±2.1, far short of the polls' D+7.7. Two cautions: the 2022 Florida mail pool was shrunk by a 2021 law that lapsed standing requests, and Republicans erased the Democratic mail lead once in-person voting opened in both 2022 and 2024; it opens Oct 19 this year, with about 1.5 million mail ballots still out. The 2024 baseline has no match until 8 days out.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 16
Call the Map (Division of Elections file), Oct 16
bullets.aff: Official data; Call the Map is an independent tracker

bullets.title: Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: National Review's Noah Rothman argues Democrats will lead the early vote, "but perhaps not by the margins the party expects," because their own warnings eroded trust in mail. Ohio Republican strategist Bob Clegg says early voting "really tells you nothing" because Republicans vote later, while acknowledging a turnout problem. Wisconsin's GOP reads the Madison and Milwaukee declines as "a lack of enthusiasm among Dem voters." No quantitative RNC early-vote claims for 2026 turned up.
bullets.aff: GOP-aligned claims, reported by nonpartisan outlets

bullets.title: Nevada opens in-person voting with a 5-point Democratic mail lead and an R+3 model.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State's count reached 41,702 mail ballots by midday Oct 16: 15,765 Democrats (38%), 13,944 Republicans (33%) and 11,993 others (29%), under 2% of active voters; the app's evening file has 46,491 at D+2.7. Jon Ralston's first run of his model projects turnout of about 1.14 million (55% of active voters) and an R+3 electorate, 39-36, with others a quarter of the vote. His benchmark for the first in-person day, Oct 17: in 2022 Clark County's day one drew 11,396 voters, 37% Democrats and 45% Republicans. In 2024 Democrats led the mail vote, Republicans led the total early vote, and Trump won; the 2024 baseline here now begins 15 days out.
sources: KSNV News 3 Las Vegas (Secretary of State data), Oct 21, 2024

calendar_note: Nevada's in-person early voting opened Oct 17; North Carolina's one-stop voting opened Oct 15; Georgia's in-person voting opened Oct 13; Minnesota's statewide early voting on tabulators opened Oct 16; Iowa and Kansas mail ballots went out Oct 14. Colorado mailed its ballots Oct 2-9; Oct 19 is when its voter service centers must open. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 39 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 12-17) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison, now resting on Florida and Iowa, is more Democratic than 2022 but implies a national vote of only about D+0.7 (±2.1) against polls at D+7.7: Florida's returned mail ballots were D+6.2 vs. D+3.7 at this point in 2022, Iowa's 1,418 absentee ballots D+45 vs. D+10, and North Carolina's files are far more Democratic than 2022's (198,547 Democrats and 90,076 Republicans vs. 131,674 and 98,173). Against 2024 every state with party registration is more Democratic, and turnout is ahead of 2022 in person in Georgia, North Carolina and Ohio while mail lags in Wisconsin, Pennsylvania and Florida, so Democrats moving from mail to in person bends every comparison; the early vote so far is consistent with a Democratic year but not with the polls' margin. The next tests are Nevada's first in-person days (Oct 17-18, against a 2022 day one that was R+8 in Clark County), Florida's in-person start on Oct 19, when its 2024 baseline is also within reach, and Colorado's first 2022 match on Oct 19.

signals.title: Georgia's in-person voting is running well ahead of 2022's pace
signals.value: More than half a million voters by 5 p.m. on Oct 15, the third day, about 6.9% of active voters, with about 21,700 mail ballots accepted; day one was 188,667 in-person votes vs. 134,962 on the first day of 2022 (70,849 in 2018), per the Secretary of State. 54% of voters so far are women; through Oct 14, 53.6% were 65 and over and 35.8% Black (GeorgiaVotes).
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Part of the in-person surge is voters who would have used mail, and at the same days out the total is below 2022 (see the other column); the 2024 first day was over 300,000.
signals.src: CBS News Atlanta (Secretary of State data), Oct 15; GeorgiaVotes, Oct 15
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state's files

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic
signals.value: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes after one week: 194,841 vs. 50,368 in 2022.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests are 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots so far.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early voters lean further Democratic than in 2024
signals.value: 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (378,000 D to 265,000 R then). 46% of 2024's Democratic early voters have already voted again, vs. 35% of Republicans. CNN/Catalist (Oct 1): voters with only Democratic primary history lead those with only GOP history by 18 points, vs. 8 in 2024.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so party is modeled, and 2024 had a presidential-year electorate.
signals.src: G. Elliott Morris (L2 data), Oct 12; CNN/Catalist, Oct 1
signals.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Catalist is a Democratic-aligned vendor

signals.title: Democrats are returning their ballots faster than in 2022
signals.value: North Carolina: 22% of Democrats' requested ballots are back, vs. 17% at this point in 2022. Pennsylvania: 20% vs. 15%.
signals.catch: It could be enthusiasm, or worry that the mail will be slow; NBC/Penn say the data can't tell yet.

signals.title: Pennsylvania's 2024 Democratic early voters are coming back faster
signals.value: 30% of the Democrats who had voted early by this point in 2024 have already voted, vs. 18% of Republicans; of about 153,000 matched early voters, 76% are registered Democrats and 17% Republicans, vs. 66% and 25% at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: L2's match covers less than half of the 346,932 ballots the state had counted by Oct 14; the official comparison (above) will supersede the party shares once the 2024 baseline reaches this point. Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year.
signals.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor

signals.title: Maine's absentee ballots are more Democratic than at this point in 2022 or 2024
signals.value: 47,497 ballots through Oct 12: 26,327 Democrats (55.4%), 8,684 Republicans (18.3%), 12,486 others (26.3%), a D+37.1 gap vs. D+35.6 at the same point in 2022 and D+25.0 in 2024; all ballots up 13% on 2022 (Democrats +11%, Republicans -1%, unaffiliated +29%) and down 21% on 2024.
signals.catch: Registration is not vote choice; the 2022 comparison is matched by working days, not calendar days, and the state's file has not been readable since Oct 16, so the count is four days old. 44% of ballots are by mail, 56% in person.
signals.src: Call the Map (Maine Secretary of State absentee file), Oct 16
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: Trump country in New Jersey is voting less Republican
signals.value: In counties Trump won by 20+, the pre-election vote has shifted nearly 11 points toward Democrats vs. this point in 2024.
signals.catch: Small counties and a presidential-year baseline.

signals.title: Minnesota's accepted ballots are running 29% ahead of 2022
signals.value: 127,682 ballots accepted in the first three weeks of voting (through Oct 8: 47,968 in person, 79,714 by mail), vs. 99,252 at the same point in 2022; 468,860 ballots distributed vs. 405,721.
signals.catch: Minnesota has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction, and its permanent absentee list has grown since 2022. Statewide early voting on tabulators only began Oct 16.

signals.title: Pennsylvania's mail vote is less Democratic than at this point in 2022
signals.value: In the 52 counties with comparable files (92% of ballots), returned mail ballots are D+48.6 by registration vs. D+55.4 at the same point in 2022 (and D+40.9 in 2024); Democratic returns are down 12% on 2022 and Republican returns up 8%, with all ballots down 7%. Statewide, 390,016 ballots through Oct 14 were 69.7% Democratic and 21.9% Republican.
signals.catch: Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year and Democrats are shifting to Election Day voting after the party's own warnings about the mail; the official comparison (above) takes over once its 2022 baseline reaches 12 days out. 67% of ballots so far are from voters 65 and over.
signals.src: Call the Map (Pennsylvania Department of State mail-ballot file), Oct 16
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the official file; affiliation not stated

signals.title: At the same days out, Georgia's total early vote is 14% below 2022
signals.value: 380,948 ballots through Oct 14 (364,670 in person, 16,278 by mail), vs. 443,696 at this point in the 2022 general election, per GeorgiaVotes' reading of the state's voter file.
signals.catch: 2022's in-person voting opened a day earlier relative to Election Day (Oct 17, 2022 vs. Oct 13, 2026), so the 2022 figure carries one more in-person day, and 2022's mail vote was several times larger. Per in-person day, 2026 is well ahead; no party registration either way.
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the Secretary of State's voter file

signals.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is running 30% behind 2022
signals.value: About 128,000 absentee ballots returned three weeks out, vs. nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022. Madison: about 9,000 vs. about 31,700.
signals.catch: No party registration; the Dane County clerk blames distrust of the Postal Service, and in-person absentee voting doesn't start until Oct 20.
signals.src: WPR, using Wisconsin Elections Commission data, Oct 13

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns have fallen back to the 2022 pace
signals.value: 440,677 ballots returned by Oct 13, vs. 432,960 at the same point in 2022; a week earlier returns were 30% ahead. Requests are up more than 20% (2,083,240 vs. 1,707,970).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. About 95% of requests come from the permanent mail list; in-person early voting opens Oct 24.

signals.title: Nevada's mail lead is 5 points, and Ralston's first model projects an R+3 electorate
signals.value: 41,702 mail ballots by midday Oct 16: Democrats 15,765 (38%), Republicans 13,944 (33%), others 11,993 (29%), under 2% of active voters. Jon Ralston's model projects turnout of about 1.14 million (55% of active voters) and an R+3 final electorate, 39-36; in 2022 Clark County's first in-person day was 37% Democratic and 45% Republican.
signals.catch: A projection, not a count: the model will be adjusted as in-person voting (from Oct 17) comes in, and Ralston says comparisons to past cycles are not useful yet. The app's official comparison starts matching 2024 at 15 days out and 2022 at 9.
